Microsoft is making significant progress in building its own cutting-edge general-purpose AI model, while also unveiling six specialized AI models at the Ignite conference. The Zhitong Finance APP has learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US) is accelerating its efforts to develop proprietary AI models. Mustafa Suleyman, head of AI at Microsoft, stated that the company is making significant progress in building its own cutting-edge general-purpose AI models, while also unveiling six specialized AI models at the Ignite conference, claiming these models can deliver comparable performance at a fraction of the cost of leading products from OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft says that some tasks that once took weeks can now be completed in minutes. Key Takeaway: From Relying on External Models to Developing In-House Competing Solutions For a long time, Microsoft's most advanced models have relied on OpenAI and other AI companies. This release demonstrates that Microsoft can develop competitive in-house technology and also shows its plan to compete aggressively on price. On Tuesday, at the Ignite conference in San Francisco, Microsoft unveiled six new AI models covering coding, cybersecurity, image generation, and speech. MAI Code 2: Microsoft claims its coding model achieves 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost; it also reaches 96% of Anthropic Claude Opus's performance while costing only 5% as much. This flagship coding model is designed to handle complex, time-consuming programming tasks, working across multiple files and understanding entire software projects. MAI Code 2 Flash: a smaller, faster model. Microsoft says its performance matches GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the latter's price; it matches Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the latter's cost. MAI Cyber 2 Flash: a cybersecurity model. Microsoft claims it outperformed GPT-6 Astra on a certain security benchmark, with a cost per task less than 2% of the latter's. Microsoft also plans to offer network-specific models to a limited customer base to help address the surge in software vulnerabilities increasingly exposed by AI tools. Other models: According to Microsoft, MAI Image 2.7 ranks first in image editing; the new transcription and real-time speech models aim to challenge leading competitors. Strategy: Leverage specialized models to gain a cost advantage Cost pressures on enterprise customers are a key backdrop to this launch. Suleiman said he keeps hearing businesses complain that "token spending is skyrocketing." He added, "Our commitment is to deliver the best price-performance ratio in the market, enabling you to truly scale your inference workloads; we also understand that you want models that are truly yours." Microsoft's strategy is to build specialized models for specific tasks, thereby achieving comparable performance at a significantly lower cost. Sulaiman said, "This basically means you're packing more tokens, knowledge, and expertise into the same number of parameters." He also stated, "This isn't just one model; it's not a flash in the pan. It's a system we've built—a machine that keeps improving over time, with performance and price being optimized in tandem." But this strategy involves a trade-off: models optimized for everyday coding tasks won't perform as well in advanced mathematics or scientific research. Moreover, Microsoft's performance largely depends on the chosen benchmarks, and some of its price advantage also reflects promotional discounts. In addition to the model itself, Microsoft also highlighted its enterprise-grade platform and cost-control tools at Ignite. Executives focused on introducing the Microsoft IQ platform, which aims to help companies organize and share employee knowledge, expertise, and tools, enabling AI systems to learn how the business operates and continuously build upon that foundation. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella emphasized that the new AI models cover scenarios such as coding, cybersecurity, and decision-making. He also highlighted Copilot Fusion, stating that it can orchestrate multiple models to deliver cutting-edge results at a significantly lower cost. Microsoft also demonstrated a model-selection feature that chooses the appropriate model for each task, managing per-request costs while maximizing output quality. Industry Background: Competition in Cutting-Edge AI Is Intensifying in Parallel While Microsoft is targeting industry leaders, cutting-edge AI itself is also evolving rapidly. On Tuesday, OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, with the new Astra priced 20% lower than the previous version. Microsoft is also advancing a cutting-edge general-purpose large language model, striving to compete across a broader range of tasks. Suleiman said Microsoft has achieved state-of-the-art pre-training results and made strong progress in reinforcement learning, but declined to provide a timeline for the model's release. He said, "My team is building true superintelligence." Potential impact: Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI may be reshaped The new model could reshape Microsoft's relationship with OpenAI and other external AI providers. MAI Code 2 will be available in GitHub Copilot, potentially shifting some coding workloads from external models to Microsoft's own models. When asked how much Copilot traffic Microsoft expects to shift to its own models, Suleyman declined to set a target but predicted that adoption would be significant. In the enterprise space, Microsoft also offers enterprise customers a licensed model weight option, allowing them to customize their models with proprietary data, but requiring deployment within Azure. Suleyman said this approach "feels like open source" while providing greater security and control. Suleiman stated that recent cybersecurity incidents—such as the breach of the Hugging Face platform by an OpenAI AI agent—have prompted him to focus not only on performance but also on critical safeguards. Ensuring that AI systems do not take harmful actions and behave as intended—known as "alignment" research—is his top priority. At the opening of the conference, Nadella also acknowledged last week's cross-regional service outage, stating that the company takes customer trust seriously, has work to do, and pledged to continue learning and improving. Going forward, the market will be focused on two key points: first, how quickly Microsoft can translate its advances in specialized AI into competitive general-purpose models; and second, whether its cost advantages are sufficient to persuade customers to switch from established rivals to Microsoft. Microsoft closed down 2.27% on Tuesday, up 5.3% year-to-date, underperforming the S&P 500. As of press time, the stock was up 0.9% in after-hours trading. title: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) Stock: Fall 2.37% Despite Major AI Security Initiative Launch - Blockonomi
content: Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) stock declined 2.37% to $505.71, losing $12.28 despite announcing a major AI security initiative. The shares retreated from intraday highs near $515 as selling pressure dominated Tuesday’s trading session. Meanwhile, Microsoft introduced new measures to strengthen AI transparency, security oversight, and corporate accountability across enterprise systems. Microsoft shares struggled throughout Tuesday’s session, although the stock recorded a modest recovery during afternoon trading. The decline came as Microsoft unveiled its AI Transparency Initiative during the company’s Ignite conference. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella presented the initiative as part of Microsoft’s broader commitment to safer AI systems. The initiative addresses growing security challenges as businesses deploy autonomous AI agents across their operations. These agents increasingly access sensitive information, corporate tools, credentials, and infrastructure without requiring approval for every action. Organizations face additional challenges when tracking decisions and verifying activities within their AI systems. Microsoft aims to establish common security standards that help businesses examine AI behavior across different platforms. The company also wants organizations to identify risks before autonomous systems execute consequential actions. Furthermore, the framework seeks to strengthen audit procedures and maintain accountability as AI adoption expands. Microsoft announced collaborations with more than 40 organizations to develop common standards for AI transparency. Partners include Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard, and Volvo Cars, alongside other companies supporting the initiative. Together, these organizations will focus on stronger verification methods, security controls, and governance practices. Microsoft will also expand its involvement in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SI Agent Standards Initiative. This participation will support research into open standards that companies can apply across different AI models. Additionally, Microsoft plans to integrate the resulting framework into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft Copilot. The integration will help customers connect AI activity records with their existing security and compliance systems. Businesses will also gain tools to assess access permissions, delegated authority, and operational risks. However, Microsoft has not provided a specific implementation schedule for every planned capability. Microsoft’s security framework focuses on three functions: visibility, independent verification, and control over AI activity. Organizations will track agent identities, authorized tasks, accessed information, and actions throughout their workflows. Moreover, independent records will help security teams verify system behavior without depending entirely on model-generated reports. The control measures will help companies enforce internal policies before AI agents perform sensitive operations. Security teams can also use activity records during investigations, recovery procedures, and regulatory audits. This approach keeps responsibility with organizations that deploy AI systems across their business operations. Microsoft designed the initiative to support both closed and open-weight models from different providers. Therefore, companies can change AI providers while maintaining consistent oversight and access controls. The announcement expands Microsoft’s enterprise security strategy, although its immediate stock performance remained negative. A dividend raise is a board putting cash behind its confidence, and four companies just did it within days of each other. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction), Quanta Services (NYSE:PWR), Spire (NYSE:SR) and Aramark (NYSE:ARMK) all lifted their quarterly payouts. Spire’s raise has the longest history: the gas utility’s increase marks its 24th consecutive year of dividend increases. Microsoft and Quanta are dividend-growth stories with small yields; Spire is a utility built for current income, and Aramark is speeding up its cash returns. Below is how well each raise is covered. Microsoft sells the software and cloud infrastructure that much of corporate America runs on: Windows, Office and Microsoft 365, and the Azure cloud platform. As Pluang reported, Microsoft raised its quarterly dividend 7.7%. Dividend records confirm the quarterly payment rising from $0.91 to $0.98, for an annualized forward rate of $3.92. Microsoft returned $10.2 billion[2] to shareholders in that quarter alone. The stock trades at a forward P/E of about 26. Risk: Spending on AI infrastructure is cutting into free cash flow. Fiscal 2026 capex jumped 79.62%[1] to $115.95 billion, and free cash flow fell 6.46% even as operating cash flow climbed. Quanta builds, upgrades, and maintains the physical networks behind the power grid, along with pipeline and communications infrastructure. Utilities and data center developers are its main customers. On an annualized basis of $0.52 and a share price of $605.03, the forward yield is about 0.09%. Quanta’s appeal is dividend growth, because the current income is minimal. Dividend safety: Few payouts are covered as heavily as this one. The annualized dividend costs roughly $78 million, about 3% of the low end of Quanta’s free cash flow guidance of $2.5 billion to $3.0 billion and about 3% of the bottom of its adjusted EPS guide of $17.90 to $18.30. Q3 free cash flow alone was $1.20 billion[3]. The dividend history matches the reported streak. Bull case: Quanta’s backlog reached a record $63.73 billion[3], Q3 revenue rose 60.1% to $12.01 billion, and adjusted EPS of $6.06 beat the $5.00 estimate. Management raised full-year guidance and pointed to an opportunity for strong double-digit adjusted EPS growth in 2027. The stock trades at a trailing P/E of about 53, and a forward P/E of about 28, so any slowdown in grid spending could hit the share price well before it threatens the dividend. Spire is a fully regulated natural gas utility serving close to 2 million homes and businesses in Alabama, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee. It raised its quarterly dividend 4.8% to $0.865 from $0.825, an annualized $3.46, payable January 5, 2027. At $87.90, Spire yields about 3.94%, the highest in this group by a wide margin. Dividend safety: The new rate equals about 86% of fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS of $4.02. That is tight, though it falls to about 69% of the low end of fiscal 2027 guidance of $5.05 to $5.25. Like most utilities, Spire spends more than it brings in: fiscal 2026 capex of $875.6 million exceeded operating cash flow of $511.8 million, and the gap is funded through capital markets and recovered through regulated rates. The track record is long. Spire has paid a cash dividend continuously since 1946, and the quarterly rate has risen from $0.6225 in 2019 to today’s level. Bull case: Spire is now a pure regulated utility after buying Piedmont’s Tennessee business and selling its marketing and storage units. Management raised its 10-year capital plan to $11.8 billion through fiscal 2036, introduced fiscal 2028 guidance of $6.10 to $6.30, and lifted its long-term adjusted EPS growth target to 6% to 8% through fiscal 2031. The forward P/E is about 15. Risk: Regulators set the pace. Spire cut its fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS outlook from a prior range of $5.40 to $5.60, citing regulatory outcomes in Tennessee and Alabama, and further disappointments would leave the payout ratio stuck near its current high level. Aramark runs outsourced food and facilities services for colleges, hospitals, stadiums and corporate campuses in 16 countries. Aramark said it raised its quarterly dividend 17% and authorized a new $1 billion share repurchase program. Dividend records show the quarterly rate going from $0.12 to $0.14, or $0.56 annualized. At $56.66, the forward yield is about 0.99%. Dividend safety: The new rate is about 25% of fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS of $2.23[4]. The annualized cost of roughly $148 million uses about 26% of fiscal 2026 free cash flow of $572.6 million[4], which management called the highest in company history. Leverage fell to 2.7x[4], the lowest in nearly two decades. The current growth run began after a reset: the quarterly rate fell from $0.11 to $0.095 in late 2023, around the time Aramark spun off its uniform business, Vestis (NYSE:VSTS), and it has been raised three times since. title: Microsoft Stock Has Grown Roughly 14-Fold Since Satya Nadella Became CEO in 2014, a 23% Annual Growth Rate. Can That Pace Continue Under Heavy AI Spending? - The Motley Fool
content: Microsoft's financial results and its CFO's reassurances should give investors confidence that its AI spending will pay off. Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft (MSFT -2.27%) in 2014, following Steve Ballmer's 14-year tenure. Ballmer managed to take Microsoft's revenue from $23 billion in the year he took over to $87 billion by the time he left. Net income climbed 135% in those 14 years. But the stock price ended up in practically the same place it was when he took over, due in part to the government's antitrust suit against Microsoft, the dot-com bubble popping, and the Great Recession in 2008. During his tenure, Nadella has focused heavily on the potential of its cloud computing business, which includes Azure and Microsoft 365. Both have produced fantastic results for Microsoft, and its Windows operating system is taking a back seat to those growing businesses these days. Overall, the stock is up more than 14-fold since Nadella took over as CEO, a 23% annualized pace. But with Microsoft spending huge sums every year to grow its data center infrastructure amid the AI boom, investors are wondering whether it can maintain that torrid pace. Microsoft's AI spending has grown considerably over the last few years. Management expects to spend $170 billion on capital expenditures this year, including $50 billion in the final three months of 2026. CFO Amy Hood says that the budget for 2027 will be even bigger. Those capital expenditures are huge bets, and making them has required Microsoft to raise outside capital. It recently sold $25 billion worth of debt at interest rates ranging from 4.85% to 6.35%. The question investors need to ask is whether Microsoft can produce returns on its invested capital above that cost of capital. Management has assured investors the answer is a resounding yes. "We feel good [about] the return on every dollar of capex we're spending. We're confident in that," CFO Amy Hood said on the company's first-quarter earnings call, answering a question about raising capital. "As we continue to improve the efficiencies of our infrastructure, each dollar of capex has the potential to support more revenue and higher returns over time." However, not all of Microsoft's AI spending will show up as Azure revenue growth. Hood noted that many resources go toward Microsoft's own products and development, which holds back potential Azure revenue growth. That shows up in its Microsoft 365 sales growth, particularly the growing adoption of Copilot. In its most recent quarterly update, Microsoft said it had 30 million paid Copilot users, but it counts over 450 million Microsoft 365 users. Both Azure and Microsoft 365 are growing quickly, and that trend is expected to continue for the foreseeable future as capex increases. Azure sales climbed 48% year over year last quarter, accelerating from 43% the quarter before. Microsoft 365 sales increased 17%, accelerating for its commercial segment. Realistically, 23% annualized share price growth is a high bar to meet. Theoretically, the stock should only increase as quickly as management improves earnings per share. In practice, however, that's rarely the case. Investors are willing to pay more or less for each dollar of earnings depending on how optimistic they are about the future. With the strong growth of Microsoft's cloud computing business and the potential for free cash flow to rise in the years following the big step-up in investment, Microsoft could retire a lot of shares while growing its overall earnings. That should result in very strong earnings-per-share growth, but 23% may be asking a lot over the medium- to long-run. But EPS growth in the high teens, combined with multiple expansion as it proves good returns on its invested capital, could result in the stock climbing by more than 20% per year for the next five years. Of course, much will depend on market sentiment and on Microsoft's ability to execute its AI development while its Azure customers continue to develop their AI applications and migrate more of their computing needs from on-premises equipment to the cloud. But with Microsoft stock trading at around 26 times forward earnings estimates, there's room for multiple expansion, and it looks like a good opportunity at this price. Ignite is more focused on enterprise customers, and Microsoft will use it to showcase its latest advancements in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, data, security, and intelligent agents. Zhitong Finance APP learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US)'s annual Ignite conference will be held in San Francisco, USA, from November 17 to 20. Unlike the Build conference, which focuses on showcasing software development tools and new technologies for developers, Ignite is more geared toward enterprise customers, and Microsoft will use it to highlight its latest advancements in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, data, security, and intelligent agents. Morgan Stanley views this year's Ignite as a key milestone for assessing the progress of Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy, rather than merely a new-product launch event. The firm maintains an "Overweight" rating on Microsoft with a price target of $650. Morgan Stanley's core conviction is that Microsoft is building an "enterprise AI flywheel" comprising Azure, Fabric, Foundry, and Microsoft 365 Copilot: Azure provides underlying computing power, Fabric integrates enterprise data and business context, Foundry helps customers select and orchestrate models and build agents, and Copilot embeds AI capabilities into employees' daily workflows. In Morgan Stanley's view, what truly deserves attention at this conference is not how many new features Microsoft unveils, but whether this technological ecosystem can be translated into more enterprise production deployments, higher product consumption, and more sustainable revenue growth. Key event schedule: Nadella's keynote speech will be held in the early hours of the 18th, Beijing time. According to the official Ignite schedule released by Microsoft, the conference will be held at the Moscone Center in San Francisco from November 17 to 20, with online events also available. The opening keynote will take place at the Chase Center in San Francisco and will be co-hosted by Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Judson Althoff. In addition, the Morgan Stanley report also lists the investor communication schedule with Microsoft's management: on November 17 at 4:00 PM Eastern Time, a session with Nadella will be held; on November 18 at 3:00 PM Eastern Time, there will be a meeting with Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood and Vice President of Investor Relations Jonathan Neilson. The above are the investor activities listed in the report and are not public keynote speeches. The enterprise AI flywheel is already backed by demonstrated results, but the key lies in whether it can continue to deliver on its promise. Morgan Stanley's optimistic assessment of Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy is primarily based on its latest quarterly results. Microsoft announced its fiscal first-quarter results for 2027 on October 28. For the quarter ended September 30, the company reported revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% year over year; operating profit increased 21% year over year, with an operating margin of approximately 50%. Azure revenue grew 48% year over year, and Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue increased 18% at constant currency. Commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $677 billion, up 73% year over year. About 30% of this is expected to be recognized as revenue within the next 12 months. This substantial order backlog provides strong visibility into Microsoft's future cloud business growth. Notably, Azure's growth is not solely driven by demand for AI infrastructure. Microsoft management stated that Foundry revenue more than tripled year over year, and increased computing power from improved GPU cluster efficiency, along with better CPU resource utilization, jointly fueled Azure's growth. Meanwhile, Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year, or 31% at constant currency. Morgan Stanley believes that Microsoft's advantage lies in its ability to integrate cloud infrastructure, data platforms, model services, and office applications, enabling enterprises to complete multiple stages—from data governance to agent deployment—within the same ecosystem. However, whether this model can truly form a closed-loop business remains to be seen and will require further evidence at this year's Ignite conference. Five Key Highlights: Copilot Monetization, Foundry Orchestration, and Compute Efficiency I. Copilot Commercialization: Shifting from Seat Growth to ARPU Enhancement Whether Copilot can further increase average revenue per user (ARPU) is one of the most important points to watch at this year's conference. Morgan Stanley believes that Microsoft's commercialization strategy is expanding from simply selling Copilot seats to three avenues: increasing the penetration of paid seats, encouraging customers to upgrade to the higher-tier Microsoft 365 E7 plan, and generating additional revenue through a usage-based billing model for agent-driven tasks. During its latest quarterly earnings call, Microsoft disclosed that Copilot's daily active users increased by nearly 50% quarter-over-quarter and more than quintupled year-over-year; the number of customers actively using pay-as-you-go Copilot Credits grew by over 75% quarter-over-quarter. Additionally, the number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats increased by more than eightfold year-over-year. This means Microsoft is trying to expand its AI business model from traditional software subscriptions to charging based on actual usage. As agents take on more workflows, corporate spending is expected to no longer be limited to the IT department's software procurement budget, but will gradually extend to the operating budgets of business units. However, Microsoft also changed the way it discloses Copilot business data in its latest fiscal quarter. The company had previously reported the number of paid seats consecutively and disclosed in July 2026 that Microsoft 365 Copilot had more than 30 million paid seats; but in the latest fiscal quarter, Microsoft did not update this figure, instead emphasizing daily active users, customer usage, and revenue momentum. Chief Financial Officer Hu De stated clearly on the earnings call that the company did not provide an update on Copilot seat numbers this quarter. Although usage metrics have increased, without the latest base figure for paid seats, it remains difficult to accurately assess to what extent the rise in user activity has translated into additional paid revenue. The shift in pricing models is also worth noting. Microsoft has launched the Microsoft 365 E7 plan at $99 per user per month, integrating products such as Microsoft 365 E5, Copilot, Agent 365, and Entra. Meanwhile, Microsoft plans to enable usage-based billing by default for newly purchased Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses sold through its cloud solution provider channel, setting a default quota of 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month. This arrangement has been adjusted to roll out gradually starting in the third quarter of fiscal year 2027, from January to March 2027. Therefore, the key question this year's Ignite needs to answer is: Can Microsoft prove that Copilot not only has more active users but can also continuously increase revenue through seat upgrades and pay-as-you-go pricing? II. Foundry: In the era of multiple models, can Microsoft control the agent orchestration entry point? If Copilot is responsible for delivering AI to end users, then Microsoft Foundry serves as the platform for developing and deploying enterprise AI applications. Microsoft said in its latest fiscal quarter that the number of Foundry customers has exceeded 120,000, with related revenue more than tripling year over year; the number of customers using multiple models to build agent solutions has increased fivefold year over year, while revenue from open-source models on Foundry has grown tenfold. Morgan Stanley believes that the growing diversity of model choices may not diminish Microsoft's platform value. On the contrary, as companies need to select among different models and adjust task allocation based on quality, cost, and response speed, a unified model management and orchestration platform could become even more important. During its earnings call, Microsoft also stated that 90% of Copilot queries use Auto mode, with the system dynamically routing between different models to balance quality, speed, and cost. This also reflects Microsoft's efforts to integrate multi-model scheduling capabilities into its own product ecosystem. What's worth watching at this year's Ignite is whether Microsoft can further showcase Foundry's actual progress in model selection, agent development, deployment, and operational management, and whether these capabilities can bring more enterprise workloads and cloud service consumption. III. Fabric: Can Enterprise Data Become a Differentiating Advantage in the AI Era? As the capabilities of foundation models become increasingly widespread, a company's true competitive advantage may increasingly hinge on its ability to enable AI to understand its own business data and workflows. Microsoft Fabric is a key component of this strategy. The platform aims to integrate enterprise data and provide intelligent agents with callable business information and context. Microsoft disclosed in its latest fiscal quarter that it has more than 44,000 paid Fabric customers, up over 50% year over year; meanwhile, more than 19,000 customers are using both Fabric and Foundry. This means that an increasing number of enterprises are beginning to integrate data platforms with AI application development platforms. Morgan Stanley believes that well-governed enterprise data and business context are key advantages that set Microsoft apart from mere model providers. If enterprises are willing to migrate more data and workflows to the Microsoft platform, the synergy between Fabric and Foundry could further drive growth in Azure consumption. IV. The widespread adoption of intelligent agents is driving demand for security; Agent 365 and corporate governance deserve attention. As AI agents evolve from answering questions to performing tasks across applications, managing their access permissions to enterprise data, tool invocations, and operational actions will become increasingly critical. Microsoft is integrating identity authentication, access control, behavior monitoring, and data protection capabilities into its agent management system. Products such as Entra, Defender, and Purview are expected to see increased enterprise demand as a result, while Agent 365 assumes the role of managing, monitoring, and governing AI agents. Microsoft had previously included Agent 365 in the Microsoft 365 E7 plan. During the latest earnings call, Nadella stated that the number of agents registered with Agent 365 has exceeded 50 million, an increase of over 30% quarter-over-quarter. For Microsoft, the growth in the number of agents not only signifies potential cloud computing demand but also indicates that enterprises need new security and governance tools. If Microsoft can integrate agent management with its existing enterprise security products, it could further encourage customers to upgrade to higher-priced enterprise software plans. V. Maia 300: Can a Proprietary Chip Reduce AI Infrastructure Costs? AI computing power demand continues to grow, and data center construction and chip procurement are also putting huge capital expenditure pressure on Microsoft. Therefore, whether self-developed chips can reduce the cost per unit of computing power is a key factor affecting Microsoft's long-term profitability. Microsoft announced its next-generation, in-house AI inference chip, Maia 300, in October and plans to scale up deployment of the Azure Maia series chips starting in 2027. The company expects that Maia 300 will deliver approximately 40% more tokens per megawatt than the previous generation, with rack-level system token throughput up to seven times that of Maia 200. However, improvements in chip performance do not necessarily translate into an immediate reduction in overall costs. Investors should continue to monitor the pace of real-world deployment, the workloads supported, and the cost and efficiency advantages relative to third-party GPU solutions. Morgan Stanley believes that as Microsoft expands its deployment of self-developed chips, improved AI infrastructure efficiency is expected to ease margin pressure and enhance the long-term returns of the Azure business. Gross margins are under pressure, but can operating leverage offset cost pressures? On the flip side of Microsoft's AI business's rapid growth is the continued rise in capital expenditures and infrastructure costs. Microsoft's capital expenditures for the first fiscal quarter reached $45.2 billion, with about three-quarters allocated to short-term assets such as CPUs, GPUs, memory, and storage. The company expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter and projects approximately $170 billion in capital expenditures for the 2026 calendar year. During the same period, the company's free cash flow was $18.6 billion. Microsoft stated that it expects to maintain positive free cash flow in fiscal year 2027, but also noted that it will continue to flexibly utilize financing channels in the future based on the cost of capital and market conditions. Morgan Stanley's model indicates that Microsoft's gross margin may gradually decline from 67.9% in fiscal year 2026 to 65.9% in fiscal year 2027, 64.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 63.5% in fiscal year 2029. However, the firm expects operating margins to remain broadly stable at 46.8%, 46.6%, 46.7%, and 47.2% over the same period, respectively. This means that Morgan Stanley expects Microsoft to offset some of the gross margin pressure from AI infrastructure investments through revenue growth, improved platform efficiency, and cost control. For investors, what truly matters is not whether gross margins decline in the short term, but whether AI investments can generate sufficient revenue and operating leverage to keep operating profit margins resilient. Behind the $650 price target: Valuation hinges on AI commercialization taking hold In terms of valuation, Morgan Stanley maintains a "Overweight" rating on Microsoft and a price target of $650. The firm's base-case scenario is based on fiscal 2028 earnings per share of $24.41, corresponding to a P/E ratio of approximately 26x. Morgan Stanley's bull-case target price is $800, based on fiscal 2028 earnings per share of $27.41 and a P/E multiple of approximately 29; the bear-case target price is $300, corresponding to earnings per share of $22.25. The bank believes that Microsoft is poised to continue expanding its enterprise AI market share through synergy among Azure, Foundry, Fabric, and Copilot. However, this assessment also implies that Microsoft must continually demonstrate that the commercialization progress of its AI products can meet market expectations for growth and profitability. The ultimate test: Can revenue growth keep pace with capital expenditures? Behind this year's Ignite, there are two conditions that must be met simultaneously: on the one hand, after Copilot expands from seat subscriptions to pay-as-you-go pricing, it must genuinely drive revenue growth; on the other hand, Microsoft must improve the utilization of its AI infrastructure to prevent capital expenditures from continuing to rise without a corresponding improvement in return on investment. In the first fiscal quarter, Microsoft's capital expenditures reached $45.2 billion, and they are expected to exceed $50 billion in the second fiscal quarter. Despite strong growth in Azure and Foundry, AI infrastructure investment remains substantial. Microsoft needs to demonstrate to the market that every additional dollar of capital expenditure generates more monetizable computing power and higher revenue returns. Therefore, the most noteworthy developments on Ignite are not any single new model or agent feature, but rather three advancements with greater commercial significance: whether Copilot can boost ARPU through seat upgrades and pay-as-you-go pricing; whether Foundry can become the core platform for enterprise agent deployment in a multi‑model environment; and whether in‑house chips and improved datacenter efficiency can reduce the cost per unit of compute. For Microsoft, the competition in enterprise AI is no longer just about model capabilities; it is also a contest of full-stack commercialization capabilities, spanning from infrastructure to applications and from data to security. Whether Ignite can present a clearer implementation roadmap will become an important window for the market to assess the return on its AI investments. title: Microsoft's (NASDAQ: MSFT) $677 Billion Backlog Makes The Case For A 24.6% Rally Despite Anthropic Pressure - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 16, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A signed commercial backlog of $677 billion gives Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) a visibility advantage that the market appears to be discounting as competitive noise crowds the headlines. Shares have drifted to around $521, sitting roughly 6.8% below the 52-week high of $559.15, even as the underlying business continues to post results well ahead of Wall Street’s expectations. The stock actually traded at $532.60 the day the October 28 earnings report landed, meaning the subsequent slide has erased those post-earnings gains and then some. Sentiment turned after Anthropic unveiled productivity tools that compete directly with Microsoft Office, including a rival to Excel, prompting MarketWatch to label Microsoft the biggest drag on the Dow. Over the past week alone, shares dropped 6.26%, adding to a 3.72% monthly decline, though the stock still holds an 8.41% gain for the year to date. The selloff looks disconnected from what the numbers actually show: fiscal Q1 2027 revenue came in at $92.279 billion, an 18.8% increase that cleared the $90.75 billion analyst estimate by a meaningful margin. Non-GAAP earnings per share of $4.89 also topped the $4.72 consensus, while operating cash flow surged 28.73% to $58 billion, and management expects free cash flow to remain positive for the full fiscal year. Azure’s 48% growth last quarter was the engine, and CFO Amy Hood signaled further acceleration, saying “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” with the division guided to expand 49% to 50% in constant currency during fiscal Q2. Beyond cloud infrastructure, foundry revenue more than tripled in the quarter, and daily Copilot users climbed nearly 50% compared to the prior quarter, reinforcing the monetization runway for Microsoft’s AI investments. Stacked against its two closest cloud rivals, Microsoft’s financial profile stands out: its 46.78% operating margin dwarfs Alphabet’s (NASDAQ: GOOGL) 32.03% and towers over Amazon’s (NASDAQ: AMZN) 11.16%, while its P/E of 29 sits well below Amazon’s multiple of 37. Google Cloud did grow 103% last quarter, but Alphabet generated negative free cash flow of $9.065 billion in the same period, a constraint that limits its capacity to compete on investment; AWS grew 39% but Amazon’s thin margins compress its valuation appeal. Against that backdrop, 24/7 Wall St. has set a 12-month price target of $648.94 on Microsoft, implying 24.6% upside from current levels, backed by a Buy rating and 90% confidence. The analyst community broadly agrees: 40 analysts rate the stock Buy and 12 rate it Strong Buy, with not one carrying a Sell recommendation on the name. The bull case extends to $748.53, a potential 43.72% return, while even the bear case of $548.36 implies a positive outcome from today’s price. Longer-dated targets from 24/7 Wall St. place the stock at $745.05 in 2028, $853.82 in 2029, and $926.15 by 2030, projections that rest on continued execution of the current AI-driven strategy. The key risks center on a planned calendar-year capital expenditure program of roughly $170 billion, operating margins expected to come in slightly below last year’s levels, and a Windows OEM revenue line guided to fall in the mid-30s percentage range. If Azure delivers on its acceleration guidance and Copilot monetization holds, the backlog alone makes it difficult to argue against the current price as an entry point. title: Over 80% Of Gateway Servers Went Dark In Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) 365 Outage That Paralyzed Outlook For Nearly A Day - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 16, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis At its worst, the disruption that swept through Microsoft’s (NASDAQ: MSFT) cloud infrastructure last week left more than 80% of servers in the affected gateway fleet completely unresponsive. The failure struck Exchange Online, the backbone of Outlook email, hardest, leaving millions of users unable to open their inboxes or receiving messages hours behind schedule. Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 applications that depend on Exchange Online also experienced degraded performance, even as portions of those platforms remained reachable throughout the incident. A preliminary incident report from Microsoft identified a software defect as the root cause, one that emerged under the combined pressure of rising user traffic and reduced available server capacity. A particularly damaging feedback loop accelerated the breakdown, as Microsoft’s own automatic rerouting systems directed users toward healthy servers, intensifying the load on whatever capacity remained functional. That cascading dynamic helped push the failure across multiple regions, turning what might have been a localized problem into a worldwide service disruption that lasted close to 24 hours. Microsoft engineers halted the spread by rolling back the faulty software change and then restoring traffic in carefully managed stages throughout Friday morning. The company confirmed that active disruptions had ended and customers were back online by 11:10 a.m. ET Friday, after which teams worked to clear the queue of emails delayed during the outage. A full incident report is expected on November 20, which analysts and enterprise customers will scrutinize for details on how Microsoft intends to prevent a single regional failure from cascading across its global network. Microsoft has already said it implemented new safeguards around how traffic gets redistributed whenever servers become unavailable, signaling an acknowledgment that the automatic rerouting mechanism itself contributed to the scale of the damage. The broader commercial question now is whether the outage prompts enterprise buyers to revisit their Microsoft 365 contracts, pushing for stronger uptime guarantees or negotiating access to backup infrastructure options. The shared architecture connecting Outlook, Teams, and Copilot means a single point of failure carries the potential to disrupt virtually every productivity tool a large organization relies on during the workday. Whether Friday’s restoration is treated as a routine recovery or a trigger for deeper scrutiny of Microsoft’s cloud resilience will likely become clearer once the final incident report lands later this month. Microsoft shares closed at US$523.88, and after a 60.3% gain over the past 5 years, the live question for investors is whether that price can be supported by the cash the business is expected to generate. The stock's next move may depend on whether the current share price lines up with what a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) view of Microsoft’s cash generation implies over time. If you are comparing Microsoft with other opportunities where cash generation plays a larger role in valuation, consider using a focused stock screen of 35 high quality undervalued stocks. The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here focuses on the cash Microsoft can return to shareholders over time and what that stream is worth in today’s money. On the latest twelve month view, the group produced roughly $97.3b of free cash flow, so the model is treating Microsoft as a business already generating very large amounts of cash rather than one that is still funding itself. Strong demand for AI workloads, including model training and inference, has driven much of this growth. Management guided to similar or slightly faster Azure growth in the next quarter. Azures performance matters because it shows that Microsofts large investments in AI infrastructure are producing revenue. For readers following Bluechip Stocks, Microsoft offers a rare combination of mature, highly profitable businesses and exposure to one of the fastest-growing technology trends. Microsofts commercial remaining performance obligation, which represents contracted revenue not yet recognized, rose sharply compared with a year earlier. A larger backlog provides visibility into future revenue, since much of it reflects long-term commitments from businesses and AI developers. Commercial bookings declined compared with last year, but that reflected unusually large commitments in the prior-year quarter. Microsoft continues to expand its Copilot AI assistant across products. Usage of its combined Copilot experience grew strongly from the previous quarter, and customers consuming Copilot through usage-based billing increased rapidly. GitHub Copilot adoption also contributed to stronger results. Premium versions of Microsofts productivity software are helping lift average revenue per user. Capital expenditures rose substantially compared with a year earlier as Microsoft invests in chips, servers and data centers. The company added many new data centers across several continents during the quarter and expects capital spending to remain elevated in the coming quarter. Management has said demand for AI capacity continues to exceed available supply. Despite this heavy investment, Microsoft continues to generate positive free cash flow and returned a significant amount to investors through dividends and share repurchases during the quarter. The scale of AI infrastructure spending is a key concern. If demand slows or pricing pressure increases, returns on these investments could fall short of expectations. Cloud gross margins have declined as the mix shifts toward AI infrastructure. The Devices and Consumer segment saw revenue decline, reflecting weakness in Windows devices and gaming. Supply chain delays for data center equipment could also limit growth. Microsofts size gives it advantages that few companies can match. It has long-standing relationships with most large enterprises through its productivity software, operating systems and cloud services. This installed base allows Microsoft to introduce AI features to millions of business users quickly, often through products customers already use every day. Its financial strength also allows it to fund massive infrastructure investments while continuing to pay dividends and repurchase shares. These factors help explain why many market watchers treat Microsoft as a primary barometer of enterprise AI adoption. In addition to partnering with external AI developers, Microsoft is developing its own first-party models. The company recently completed pre-training of its next base model and released a structured decision-making model that quickly gained thousands of customers. Building in-house models gives Microsoft more control over costs, capabilities and product integration, and reduces dependence on any single partner. These models are being integrated into Microsofts products, including Copilot, Azure AI services and business applications. Combining proprietary models with access to third-party models on Azure allows Microsoft to offer customers a wide range of options while capturing value from AI usage across its platform. Microsoft is also improving how quickly new AI systems go live in its data centers, reducing the time between equipment arriving and capacity becoming available to customers. Faster deployment helps the company convert its large capital investments into revenue more quickly. Microsofts latest quarter shows strong momentum in Azure, a rapidly growing backlog and expanding Copilot usage. These trends suggest enterprise AI adoption is moving from experimentation to large-scale deployment. The central question is whether Microsoft can sustain this growth while managing the costs of one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in its history. Its results over the coming quarters will remain an important signal for the broader AI market. title: Has Microsoft Stock Become A Different Bet? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Microsoft (MSFT) stock trades at 27.3 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. At that price you want to know exactly what you own, and the company’s priorities have moved. During its fiscal Q2 2025 call in January 2025, management talked up customers such as UBS moving workloads to Azure, and it still made the case for cloud migrations a year later. On its October 2026 call, management emphasized something else. What does management talk up now instead? Management now emphasizes Foundry, the platform customers use to build AI agents and deploy them at scale, calling it an increasingly important driver of growth. On the October 28, 2026 call, management said Azure revenue grew 48% in fiscal Q1 2027, driven by Foundry and by earning more from its CPU capacity. A cloud migration moves a customer’s existing work onto Azure, Microsoft’s cloud. On the fiscal Q4 2025 call in July 2025, management said Azure had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%. Investors paying a premium for Microsoft appear to be betting that Azure can keep growing on new AI work rather than on workloads moved over from elsewhere. So far management has named Foundry as a driver of Azure’s growth in fiscal Q1 2027, though it said that growth also spanned core cloud services. Management said on the July 29, 2026 call that Azure passed $100 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, up 41%. Microsoft’s total revenue passed $331 billion that year, up 18%, so Azure grew more than twice as fast as the company. That gap held in the latest quarter. Microsoft’s revenue rose 18.8% in fiscal Q1 2027, well short of Azure’s pace. Foundry is growing faster still. Microsoft now has more than 120,000 Foundry customers, and management said Foundry revenue more than tripled from a year earlier. Foundry feeds a cloud business already worth more than $100 billion a year. On growth, the shift looks reassuring. You also want to know what the data centers behind that growth cost. In fiscal Q1 2027, Microsoft’s cash from operations rose to $58.0 billion from $45.1 billion a year earlier. Yet as reported, fiscal Q1 2027 free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, fell to $18.6 billion from $25.7 billion a year earlier. Management expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, against $45.2 billion in fiscal Q1. That measure counts finance leases in full when each lease starts. The cash Microsoft paid for property, plant and equipment in Q1 was $39.4 billion. Management’s guide for the full fiscal 2027 is that Microsoft will remain free cash flow positive, and management said it will tap additional sources of funding when it finds them attractive. At the end of September 2026, Microsoft held $64.3 billion of cash and short-term investments, more than its $57.2 billion of debt. So Foundry is one named driver of Azure’s growth so far, while the cash that pays for the data centers is the weaker side. If free cash flow falls further, holders own a faster-growing Microsoft that keeps less of its sales as cash. Azure growth, against management’s guide of 49% to 50% in constant currency for fiscal Q2 2027, and free cash flow are the two numbers to watch when Microsoft reports in January 2027. To stay a Microsoft shareholder, you mostly need to believe that cloud, Microsoft 365, Copilot and Azure driven AI services remain central to how enterprises run critical work. According to CubanEros, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the key question is whether elevated AI capex near 37% of revenue earns solid returns without stressing the balance sheet, which is currently supported by net cash and high returns on equity. Right now, the most important short term catalyst is how quickly Microsoft converts that AI infrastructure into usage across Azure, Copilot and enterprise contracts. The recent Microsoft 365 outage is a reputational issue, not a clearly material hit to demand so far. However, reliability will hang over renewal conversations and could sharpen scrutiny of capital allocation and operational execution. The IBM partnership on Imagine Enterprise looks closest to the outage debate because it ties Microsoft’s AI stack directly into highly regulated industries where governance, security and reliability are non negotiable. This platform leans on Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft 365 infrastructure, Entra and Purview. These are the same layers customers now expect to be resilient after the disruption. For investors watching catalysts, Imagine Enterprise gives Microsoft another route to embed AI agents into real workflows, with IBM Consulting bringing thousands of pre built agents and transformation projects. Execution risk sits in rolling these projects into production at scale without adding complexity or downtime. That consideration matters even more after a high profile resilience test like the recent outage. CubanEros anchors a fair value of US$419.91 on Microsoft by assuming revenue expands at 10.2% a year and that the business eventually supports a future profit margin of 39.3%, which together indicate meaningful earnings power once current AI capex rolls into mature returns. Uncover how Microsoft's fair value indicates a 20% potential downside to its current price, suggesting that the apparent premium may prove fragile. Some of the lowest Microsoft analysts fixate on margin risk rather than outages. They already penciled in revenue of US$552.2b and earnings of US$185.7b by 2029, yet still saw room for profit compression and a P/E near 25.9x. After a reliability shock like this, that cautious story could easily get sharper.
